translations.text: Blessed is God, who wills that all people be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth,
who by his ineffable providence ordains what is best for all,
and by his unfathomable goodness reveals, in each age, those who are worthy and pleasing to him, for the benefit of the human race and for the glory of his Godhead.
In these our own times, too, he has revealed our blessed fathers:
John and Euthymius, and John, and Arsenius, bishop of Ninotsminda, and John Grdzelisdze, and after them, one after another, their other disciples and imitators of their virtue,
whose names are written in the book of life.
Through their intercession may the Lord make us wretched ones worthy, too, to imitate their virtues and to attain the portion of those on the right hand.
Length of time brings everything to oblivion. It is true that before God everything is clear and manifest, and he knows the beginning and the end of all things,
and those who completed their lives in a way pleasing to him shine before him forever, and they have no need at all of being remembered by us.
Yet his all-wise providence has ordained that divine things should also be written down in books:
the all-beautiful works of the creation of the world, his lordly commandments and ordinances, and the all-praised lives and ways of life of his worthy and blessed servants,
whom his goodness saw fit to reveal in each age for the benefit of the human race,
so that through those divine and lofty works we might be stirred to glorify him and to long for him, and through those lordly ordinances we might be enlightened and become eager to fulfil them,
and so that, by remembering his great servants who were his own, we might come to emulate and imitate their divine way of life, which, like speaking images,
is set before everyone who wishes to enter eternal life as a model of virtue, a teaching of wisdom, and a source of strength and fortitude.
From the beginning of the world until now, as the written books show, the saints who shone forth and struggled, and whose lives, contests and labours were written down,
are remembered with honour in the holy churches and are worthy of prayer and blessing.
Since, then, these blessed fathers of ours mentioned above were in no way inferior to the saints who appeared earlier,
but were adorned with every virtue and fulfilled the commandments of God,
we did not think it right to leave their life unrecorded, and my spiritual fathers also commanded me to undertake this.
Therefore I entreat your worthiness, God-clad fathers, that I not be held to blame on this account.
And although we have undertaken to write these few words long after they departed to God,
let no one doubt them, for we have written nothing of our own invention, only what we learned from trustworthy men and spiritual fathers
who had seen these fathers and served them, and who were entirely free of falsehood and full of grace from above;
and from their very works, which bear silent witness and loudly proclaim their contests and labours:
This lavra, glorious, adorned with every beauty and made beautiful with every ornament, which those blessed men built with much labour and sweat as a place of rest for many souls,
in which they raised up churches that imitate the heavens. They filled them with God-inspired books and made them shine with precious icons.

They acquired villages, estates, monasteries and hermitages for it. They laid down rules and canons for it, glorious and altogether beautiful, and they secured it with confirmations and gold-sealed charters from God-serving kings.
They gathered monks and religious into it, imitators of the angels, and they adorned our language and our land and made them flourish with translations of the holy Scriptures,
so that from here, truly, the law and the word of the Lord went forth as from Zion, as from Jerusalem, according to the word of the loud-voiced Isaiah.
For truly worthy and beloved of God was our blessed father John, who, like Abraham,
chose exile and a life of pilgrimage and poverty, and gave himself in obedience to spiritual fathers. Therefore, also like him [Abraham],
God glorified this man too and made him renowned for every virtue, and above all by granting him that most blessed son, who is the blessed Euthymius,
whose name alone is enough to show the height of his virtues. He appeared as an ornament of our nation and an imitator of the holy apostles.
He enlightened the language and the land of the Georgians. For, as the colophons written in the books he translated testify,
through the efforts of this worthy man [John] he was instructed in all wisdom, to be an enlightener and adorner of our churches.
His labour gladdens those far and near, and the sweetness of the books he translated resounds through every land like a loud-voiced golden flute,
not only in Kartli but in Greece as well, for he translated Balavar, Abukura and a number of other writings from Georgian into Greek.
But I will first say only what I had intended to say above, and afterwards I will tell you in brief words whatever the Lord may grant us.
For we have come to these last days and, as you see, great coldness is to be seen among us.
Let no one, then, think and deceive himself that our brothers were like this from the beginning.
Far from it! Rather, they lived with all orderliness and in a godly way of life
for as long as those thrice-blessed fathers of ours, John and Euthymius, governed and held the office of abbot.
In every way they led the flock entrusted to them like those first God-clad fathers.
But when blessed John went to his rest and our God-clad father Euthymius withdrew from the office of abbot, from then on every kind of faintheartedness and coldness increased among us.
But let us pray to God that, through their intercession, he may govern this life of ours well too, and not leave us deprived,
nor separate us from the joy and rest of those blessed fathers and brothers of ours in the eternal life.
But let us return to our first subject. This blessed father of ours, John, was a Georgian by birth,
Glorious and distinguished from his parents and grandparents, and eminent among the princes of David the Curopalates, brave and valiant, renowned in battles,
tall and handsome in stature and in the build of his body, and wise and intelligent in mind and understanding,
and full of the fear of God and of every good work, and greatly beloved by and close to David the Curopalates of blessed memory.
But since the fire of the love of Christ blazed fiercely in his heart,
he despised all the glory of this world and counted it as refuse: possessions and wealth and ease, his wife and his children and kinsfolk, and
whatever belongs to this world, he utterly hated and disregarded, and then also his own self, according to the word of the Lord,
and he took up the cross upon his shoulders. In secret from everyone he took to flight, separated himself from all, and alone entered the glorious lavra of the Four Churches (Otkhta Eklesia).
Those who shone there in virtue at that time were Father Moses and Father Gelasius.

To them he revealed who he was, and from them he secretly received the blessing of monkhood. For some time he gave himself over to obedience with mighty struggle and amazed all the ascetics who were there.
But since his deeds began to become known, he received the prayer of those blessed fathers and set out for the land of the Greeks, for he was fleeing the glory of men.

And so he reached Mount Olympus, and in a certain monastery, for no little time, he valiantly took upon himself the labour of tending the mules, and with humility carried out other lowly and despised services.
But since in those times the emperor of the Greeks gave the upper lands to David the Curopalates and demanded the sons of nobles from him as hostages,
the brothers of Father John's wife brought his son Euthymius to the emperor as a hostage, together with other princes' sons.
When John learned this, he had no choice but to reveal who he was against his will, and he went up to the imperial city.
And since the emperors knew Abuharb, who was the father-in-law of Father John, they also showed John great love on that account and received him kindly.
And after this there was a prolonged dispute between John and his father-in-law over Euthymius, for he did not want to give him up.
And John reproached him severely: "What is this? Do you perhaps not have sons of your own?
But this is clear: you had mercy on them as your own children, and my son, as though he were an orphan, you gave up as a hostage!
But may the Lord forgive you!" And so, by divine providence and by the judgement of the emperors, he took his own son and returned again to Olympus.
But after some time, since his name became renowned and both Greeks and Georgians honoured him, this grieved him, and for this reason he again went off into life as a stranger in foreign lands.
For he took his son and some disciples and came to the Holy Mountain, to the lavra of the great Athanasius. And there he was received.
He kept who he was hidden, and he did every task of obedience with humility and without complaint. He spent two years or more working as a cook.
And in those times his kinsman, the great Tornike, became a monk in his own country, and since he had heard about John,
that he was at Olympus. Since he had great love for him, he set out toward him and came down to Olympus, and since he did not find him there,

he searched carefully in secret and learned that he was on the Holy Mountain. Without the emperors knowing, he came secretly to the Holy Mountain and received the blessing of monastic profession from the hands of John.
For, as we said, he came down to the Holy Mountain and reached the lavra of the great Athanasius, and since concealment was no longer possible,
they made themselves known to one another and were joined in spiritual love, and there was great joy in the monastery that day,
for the great Athanasius also knew of Tornike's deeds, his eminence and his valour.
For this reason he held them in great honour from then on. Although they did not want this, God reveals and glorifies those who are worthy of him.
After some time their story spread and it became known that they were on the Holy Mountain. From then on Georgians began to come there and to grow in number.
When our blessed fathers saw this, being full of all wisdom, they took counsel together and said:
"It is not right for us to remain in the monastery, for others are also coming to us, and distraction by outside affairs is impossible [for us to bear]."
So, on the advice of father Athanasius, at a distance of about one mile from the lavra,
in a beautiful wilderness, they built a church of Saint John the Evangelist and cells, and they lived there for a long time like angels of God.
At that time the rebellion of Sclerus took place. He seized the whole mainland, and the emperors and the empress were shut up in the City in great distress and hardship.
While they were in this situation, they took counsel and said: "We have no helper apart from David the curopalates."
Since Sclerus had seized all the roads, it was not possible to send a man,
and they were in great anxiety, for there was no man suitable to carry out what they wished.
While they were troubled about this matter, they heard about John and Tornike and learned that they were at the lavra of the great Athanasius.
At once they sent the sebastophoros, a man of high rank at that time among the empress's officials, to the Lavra with imperial letters.
When he arrived, he gave the letters to each of them separately, as he had been ordered: one to Athanasius, one to Tornike and one to John.
This is what was written: "The godless Sclerus has rebelled against us and has seized the whole mainland.
Now we beseech your holiness that John Tornike come to our majesty without any excuse."
Many other entreaties and urgent requests were also written in those imperial letters.
When this happened, Athanasius and John were left completely helpless. Whether they liked it or not, they fell at Tornike's feet and began to beg him to go up before the emperors.
But when he heard their plea, he was deeply distressed and said to them: "Holy fathers,
I have come to this holy place because of my sins, and it is impossible for me to go before the emperors, for I know for what purpose they are summoning me, and
since God has made me worthy and I have put on the monastic habit, from now on I have nothing more to do with the emperors, or with anyone else on earth.
"Now I beg your holiness, for the love of God, forgive me and do not force me in this matter, for if I go, they will throw me back into the turmoil of this very world."
And they pleaded with him, saying: "If at this time we disobey the emperors, we will bring great wrath down on ourselves and on this monastery."
And a whole week passed in this dispute.
But in the end, whether he wished it or not, Father Athanasius and Father John took all the blame on themselves, and with difficulty they persuaded him to go.
Now Basil and Constantine were at that time still young boys, and the whole government was in the hands of the empress and the parakoimomenos.
And as soon as Tornike went up to the imperial city, the parakoimomenos immediately brought him before the emperors.
And the emperors and the empress rose to their feet for him, greeted him with honour, and seated him beside them. And the empress gave an order to Basil and Constantine, and they fell at his feet.
And the empress said to him: "Holy father, whatever you do for these orphans, may God repay it to your soul!"
And when such an occasion came to John, he rebuked the empress frankly [?] about many kinds of matters.
And she accepted it all with humility and promised him: "Holy father, whatever your fatherhood commands me,
I will not go against your command. Only, may God strengthen you, take this labour upon yourself and, by whatever means you wish,
go before the curopalates and tell him of all our distress, and I trust in God that you will drive out that godless Sclerus and deliver us from distress."
He begged the empress earnestly to release him. And when he saw her firmness, he answered thus:
"I put on this habit because of my sins, and the Lord knows that this task weighs on me as heavily as death.
But what am I to do? I do not know. I cannot disobey your holy majesty." And again the empress and the parakoimomenos said to him:
"Only stretch out your hand to these orphans, and whatever sin there may be, may God require it of us." And so letters of supplication were written to the curopalates.
And so he took leave of the emperors, and by whatever way he could, Tornike reached the presence of the curopalates.
The curopalates rejoiced greatly and received the emperors' letters, and Tornike explained the whole matter to him,
for which reason they made a plan to send troops to Byzantium, and they appointed Tornike as commander-in-chief.
And Tornike sent letters from the curopalates and from himself to the emperors and informed them of all the curopalates' wishes.
And then the emperors gave the upper lands of Byzantium to the curopalates, for him to hold for his lifetime.
And to Tornike they wrote: "We know that God will help you, so do not doubt at all; and when God grants you success, take captive all our opponents, and all the spoil taken from them shall be yours."
For this reason the curopalates gave Tornike twelve thousand picked horsemen.
And with the help of Christ he drove off Sclerus and put him to flight as far as Persia.

And then he returned and, according to the word of the emperors, took captive all the nobles of Byzantium and plundered their possessions; some of the spoil he divided among the troops, and some he kept for himself, a very great quantity of spoil:
gold and silver and silk brocade and other such things. And he turned back, and greeted the curopalates and thanked him greatly, and took his leave, and came again before the emperors.
And they met him with great honor and greeted him warmly.
Then he parted from them too and took his leave. And he returned again to the Holy Mountain, to the lavra of the great Athanasius.
And the fathers met him with joy and embraced him and gave thanks to God, who had brought him back again in peace.
And after this our fathers took counsel and said: "It is impossible for us to stay here; we are men of renown, and Georgians are coming to us."
And they decided this: that they would build their own monastery apart, independently.
Although this matter was hard for John, yet for the repose of the Georgians, and above all to satisfy Tornike, he took the undertaking upon himself.

And by the grace of God they found a beautiful place in the middle of the Holy Mountain, and with much sweat and toil they built a monastery and churches in the name of the holy Mother of God and of the holy John the Baptist.
And they bought with their own money many places, monasteries and hermitages around the great monastery, as far as the sea on the other side,
which are beautiful and desirable and suitable for spiritual monks to dwell in.
And likewise the God-serving emperors, since they had rendered them such services and done great deeds for them, whatever places and villages they asked for,
the emperors confirmed them all with chrysobulls; and these are many and very choice, as befits this land.
And while Tornike was in the East, he brought back many [?] and renowned monks, a multitude not small, and he wished
that only Georgians should be all the inhabitants of this monastery; but since this was impossible to do, they were compelled to bring in Greeks as well,
for we, as you see, have no experience whatsoever of the sea, and everything we need comes in by sea;
and moreover, without smiths and carpenters and masons and vinedressers and shipbuilders and others of this kind, it is impossible to maintain so large a lavra as this.
And our holy fathers considered all this, and whether they wished it or not, as we have said, they accepted them too.
And so with God's help the building of the monastery was completed. And Tornike, since he had defeated Skleros and had returned here again with countless wealth and treasure,
for he brought more than twelve kentenaria in treasure alone, apart from other fine things,
all of which he gave into the hands of his spiritual father John, and he renounced himself completely and did not keep even the smallest thing under his own authority;
but that man, so famous and illustrious, cut off all his own will and gave himself wholly to obedience to John.
And he showed such fervor that, had it been possible, he would not have tasted even water without John's command, nor uttered a single word, nor been master of even a single obol;
but Father John managed everything and gave it out as he wished and wherever it was needed.
And since the head of all the virtues is obedience to spiritual fathers and the cutting off of one's own will, and he had this, just as we have told your love of God,
And still more exceedingly so, for with weeping he would confess even his trivial thoughts to the blessed John, and ask for a penance and for forgiveness.
We have deliberately passed over a detailed account of his other virtues, for truly this blessed man was full of every virtue:
humility, simplicity and innocence. And he would always say to the great John:
"Father, you yourself know that I am a great sinner, and my death is near, and I do not stand outside the will of your holiness;
rather, after God, I have given my will and my very self over to you. Save my soul as you see fit."
When our blessed father John saw such fervour in him, he took great care
that he should lack nothing whatsoever. He paid him fitting honour, treated him with deference, gave him rest, and showed compassion for his old age.
But because the great Tornike had been brought up amid battles and military affairs, he loved to talk and tell stories about such matters,
and, as we have said, Father John treated him with deference and did not want to rebuke him, so as not to wound his feelings.
And since there were at that time distinguished and honourable men there, they would go in to him and talk with him about the matters mentioned above.
Then, when John saw that he did this out of simplicity, he became afraid that in this way some spiritual harm might come to that worthy man, and to his own soul as well.
For this reason Father John said to him: "Beloved brother, I see
that by the grace of God you have made good progress in God's commandments, and I do not want to bring some harm on your soul by holding back out of deference.
So now stop talking about those worldly matters, and from now on speak with no one else except Gabriel the priest."
That priest was the kind of man from whose mouth no worldly word ever came; everything he said was divine and spiritual.
When the worthy man heard this, he immediately fell at his feet and said with tears:
"Then why did you keep silent until now and not rebuke me, holy and God-clothed father?" But Father John raised him up and said to him:
"May the Lord forgive you; only be careful from now on." And from then on he no longer spoke with any of the brothers of the monastery. But if some stranger came, he would answer him a few words.
And so he completed his days in this spiritual way of life and went to God. And our fathers truly bore witness concerning him that
"God has forgiven his sins and made him worthy of eternal life."
These worthy and blessed fathers of ours donated great wealth and many fine things to the Great Lavra and to all the monasteries of the Holy Mountain,
which at that time were still poor and not as numerous as they are now.
And to the Mese, which is the meeting place of the whole Mountain, they gave many utensils and possessions.
And they distributed much wealth to everyone, both to the community as a whole and to each person individually. We will mention some of these gifts and leave out the rest,
so that this writing does not grow too long and we do not become tiresome to readers and listeners.
As we said, they gave the Great Lavra a chrysobull (a gold-sealed charter) granting a treasury allowance of two hundred and forty-four drachmas. Tzimiskes had granted it to John,
and the Lavra receives this from the palace every year. They also gave the island called Neoi, which Emperor Basil had likewise granted to John,
and which yields an income of 14 litras every year, or fifteen, and sometimes even twenty.

Again, they gave 25 litras of counted gold as a treasury. They also gave a relic of the Wood of Life in a silver case, two large silver chalices, and a paten with a spoon, an asterisk [?], and a silver reliquary.
All of these were gilded. There was also an altar covering embroidered with gold, and a second one of oxinon [?].
There were two books of Chrysostom, the Margaritai ("Pearls"); another book of Saint Ephrem; another book, the Teachings of Saint Cyril;
another book in which all the old books (the Old Testament) are written, together with the Prophets and the Maccabees;
another book, the festal book of the illustrious saints; and a Gospel book covered in brocade, with silver bosses and a cross.
There was a gilded silver processional cross with enamel images, and a large wax-painted (encaustic) icon of the Crucifixion valued at a hundred drachmas.
There was another large icon of the Deesis; another icon of the Deposition from the Cross, given by Emperor Nicephorus; and another icon, a templon (icon beam) of the Twelve Apostles;
another icon of the holy great martyrs; another wax-painted icon of the Baptist; and another wax-painted icon of Saint Eustratius.
They also gave a hundred litras of aloeswood, four mules, three horses, and a ship of five hundred modii.
They also spent money on building the cells: five hundred drachmas on the upper ones, a hundred drachmas on the lower ones, and other such things.
We have written all of this from the list in the hand of the holy father Euthymius himself, so it is true and free of falsehood.

Likewise, in the 8th indiction they gave the Mese (the central assembly) fourteen litras as a treasury, to be distributed among everyone. Again, in the 11th indiction they distributed another 14 litras.
To the church of Karyes, the gathering place of all, they gave a gilded silver chalice and paten decorated with images,
and a templon of the Feasts of the Lord, a Commentary on the Gospel, three large Deesis icons, two skaramangia (ceremonial robes), and two mules.
They gave the steward of the Mese one litra as a treasury for the Mese, to be spent on buying chandeliers, dragon-shaped lamps [?], chains and candles.
Again, after the death of Tornike, in the 13th indiction, they gave the Mountain twenty-eight litras to be distributed.
At Hierissos they gave houses, bought for seven litras, together with an enclosing wall, as lodging for traveling brothers. They also gave a choice vineyard there, valued at five litras.
We have also written all of this from the written record of our fathers.
But who could count what was given to each individual person? Each one of them proclaims it aloud, and God has recorded it in heaven!

Apart from what is written above, Father Euthymius also gave two hundred drachmas to the Mese for his own monastery of Saint Euthymius. He built this monastery outside on the Mountain after he stepped down as abbot.
Here, then, let us stop speaking on this subject. As we said, it is not even possible to tell one by one all of their good works,
for more than any other virtue they had grown fond of almsgiving and had put it on like a garment.
After Tornike's death, our blessed father John decided to take his son and some of his disciples and flee to Spain.
For from the beginning he had hated strife and turmoil, but he had put up with it until then for the sake of Tornike's building work, and so that he might win his soul,
for he had heard that Georgians, no small race and people, live there.
For this purpose he went as far as Abydos, so that he might find a ship there bound for the regions of Spain and go there.
The man who governed Abydos at that time was very dear to father John, and because of their friendship John told him what he intended.
But he opposed him and hindered him as far as he could.
When he saw that father John stood firm in his intention, he spoke openly and said to him:
"Holy father, you know how much the emperors love your worthiness. If I let you go, great harm will come upon me.
Write to the emperors, and do as they command."
When he wrote to them, the emperors ordered that they be sent to the imperial city.
When they went up there, the emperors received them with great honour, but strongly reproached them and said:
"Holy fathers, we have great love for your holiness. What is this, that you flee from us like this and go to a foreign land?"
The blessed John answered and said: "God-serving and sovereign emperors, I, this poor man, was a layman living in the world and guilty of every sin, and I wished
to go away into some foreign land, save my soul, and live in poverty. How it came about, I do not know:
my kinsman Tornike came, and through him I fell into great strife and into crowds of people. I wish to be free of all this and to devote myself to the care of my soul."
For a long time they kept him there with great honour. Then, with much pleading, they barely persuaded him to return to the monastery, and they sent him away with great gifts.
And so he went back again to his own monastery.
A short time later he fell ill with gout. For many years he lay bedridden on a couch and endured severe pain.
He always gave thanks to God, and in that cruel illness he was as joyful as if over great wealth, or over honour and a royal gift.
When he saw how weak he had become, he begged father Euthymius to take on the care of the monastery.
But Euthymius reverently pressed him to excuse him, for he hated the turmoil of this world and would not consent to fall into such turmoil.
But since it was impossible to disobey an aged father worn down by illness, he had to obey him, whether he wanted to or not. And while John was still in the flesh,
Euthymius managed the affairs of the monastery as steward, in obedience to John and under his orders, and did nothing without his command.
At that time the blessed and holy elder John Grdzelisdze was living like a bodiless being, in seclusion, in the Lavra of the Four Churches.
Likewise Arsenius of Ninotsminda, a man lofty in virtue and a worker of Christ's commandments, who for God's sake gave up his bishopric and came to David the Curopalates,
And he, of blessed memory, greeted him as his holiness deserved and sent him on to Otkhta Eklesia (the Four Churches).
And so he too lived in seclusion with his own teacher.
These blessed fathers of ours, John and Arsenius, had great love for one another, and for a long time they labored there in the good struggle of the monastic life.
But they saw that they could not live the quiet life as they wished, because the abbots and the brothers of the monastery troubled them,
and the curopalates also wrote to them again and again and sent them eulogia (blessed gifts), and so did the bishops and the nobles.
For this reason they decided to go away to a foreign land.
So they went to deserted places in the region of Pontus and met a certain spiritual abbot,
who received them with joy and gave them a beautiful monastery in a deserted place, and generously gave them everything they needed.
And after some time our fathers learned about them, that they were living there.
And they sent a brother and wrote them letters, saying: "Holy fathers, we have heard about your holiness and have learned that you are living there, and we are very disheartened
that you did not wish to come to this holy and renowned mountain, so that we might have received your holy prayers.
Now we beg your holiness to come, so that we may live together, since you know that we too are living in a foreign land."
When they read this, they too were pleased, and in the second year they came down. And when our fathers learned of it,

they were filled with joy and gave thanks to God, and they greeted them warmly and provided for them spiritually and bodily as they wished, and built cells for them in a deserted place, and they lived a way of life pleasing to God.
After this our blessed father John, worn out by the illness mentioned earlier,
reposed and went to God, enriched with a burden of virtues and a doer of God's will.
And when he was about to die, he gave all authority and power to father Euthymius, so that whatever order and rule he wished,
he might lay down for the monastery and set canons over it, and govern it within and without as he wished.
And then he commanded that after himself he should leave the abbacy to George, who was one of their own, a man of renown and careful in bodily affairs.
And again he commanded that George, after him, should leave another as superior, whoever should be found better than the others among the brothers in word and deed.
And so he laid down that each abbot, after his own death, should leave another superior, worthy and virtuous.
But if anyone should be found who breaks the order of father Euthymius, and who causes disturbance and opposes the brothers,
he condemned such a person with a curse and a terrible anathema, cast him away from God, and commanded
that such a person be driven out of the community at once, so that his deadly and corrupting disease would not spread through the whole body of the community.
And he appointed the autocrat emperors as administrators and guardians, and said:
"Since one needs someone to show favour, to give a helping hand and to manage things, what am I to do, this poor and worthless man?
For although this is a bold thing to say, I trust in their sweet mercy and goodness.
I entrust this lavra, which I built through their favour and help, into their own hands, together with my fellow servants and their intercessors, Euthymius and George.
For although they show mercy to the whole land and care for all the poor, they have shown more mercy to us, unworthy as we are, than to anyone else.
That is why I was able to build this lavra from its foundations through their great benefactions."
And to the brothers he said: "You, my dear and beloved children,
if you strive to keep God's commandments and live according to the rule and the divine canon, and show blameless obedience to your superiors, and keep peace and unity with one another,
I believe in God that God will not let you lack any good thing. Rather, he will move kings, princes and all people to show you mercy, and you will advance more and more.
From now on, let no one separate you from this good work, which is dear to God: blameless obedience and unbroken unity and peace.
Then you will live out an untroubled life in this passing world, and in the age to come you will inherit eternal life, through the love for humankind of Christ the King.
And may the good and most merciful God show you mercy and guide you in his holy will and his divine commandments,
through the intercession of the all-holy Mother of God and of all the saints. Amen.
Do not forget hospitality. Whatever God grants you, give to the poor as far as you are able. And pray for me and remember me, my beloved children and brothers,
always, so that God may show mercy to my pitiable soul, which grew up in sins, and forgive me all my sins.
Remember also our spiritual brother John the Synkellos, for he came to us on this holy mountain with great faith.
And each year keep the commemoration of our spiritual father Athanasius and remember him in the holy liturgies."

When he had said all this and left it in writing, he gave the blessed Euthymius a blessing from on high. Into Euthymius's hands he committed his holy soul to God, and then he lay down in peace and fell asleep
on the 14th of June. He is an intercessor for the salvation of our souls.
Our God-clad father Euthymius clothed his honoured body as was fitting, buried it with his own hands, and built over it the church of the holy Archangels.
And those who come to it in faith are made worthy of grace and comfort.
For once a man possessed by a demon came to it and drank from the lamp that hung over his tomb. He was healed at once and glorified God.
But let us return to our earlier account. As we said above, the father, John, took his son Euthymius away from the imperial court.
First he taught him Georgian learning, and then he had him fully educated in Greek in every branch of learning.
From his childhood the grace of God was upon him. God gave him understanding of the Scriptures, and he was filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit.
As it was made known to blessed John, his father, through a revelation of the holy Mother of God: in the time of his youth,
while he was still a boy, he was seized by a severe illness and came near to death. And blessed John used to say:
"I gave up hope for his life, for I expected his soul to depart at any moment, since neither speech nor voice remained in him any longer. And as I was greatly distressed,

I went to the church of the holy Mother of God and fell down before the icon of the holy Lady, and with hot tears I implored the incorruptible, ever-virgin Mother of God to be his helper and to grant him relief.
And I instructed the priest to come up quickly and give him communion of the Body and Blood of the Lord.
And as I was distressed and hurried to see what had happened, I opened the door of the cell where I had left him lying,
and at once I smelled a wonderful fragrance, for the holy Mother of God had looked upon him, and I saw Euthymius,
for by her grace he had risen and was sitting on the bed, completely healthy and unharmed.
And as my mind was astounded, I asked him, "What is this, son?" He answered me and said:
"Just now a glorious Lady appeared before me and said to me in the Georgian language, 'What is it? What ails you, Euthymius?' And I said to her, 'I am dying, Lady.'
And when I had said this, she came close to me, took hold of my hand and said to me, 'There is nothing wrong with you. Get up, do not be afraid, and speak Georgian fluently.'
And behold, as you see me, nothing ails me any longer at all." And blessed John used to say:

"Until that time he spoke Georgian with difficulty, and I was very troubled on this account; but from then on [his speech] flowed forth unceasingly like a spring, more purely than that of all Georgians.
And I, when I saw this, fell down before the holy Mother of God and offered thanks to her who is our hope, and I gave thanks to God and glorified him. Amen."
Father John used to say to him: "My son, the land of Kartli is greatly lacking in books, and many books are missing; and I see that God has granted you grace.
Now strive, so that you may increase your reward from God."
And he, as he was obedient in all things, promptly followed his command and began to translate, and he amazed everyone,
for such translation, apart from those earlier ones, has not appeared in our language, and I think it will not appear again.
And he sent many books to David the curopalates; and when he saw them, being a man of faith, he was filled with joy, glorified God, and said:
"Thanks be to God, who in these times of ours has revealed a new Chrysostom." And he wrote to him again and again that he should keep translating and sending [books].
And that blessed man translated without rest and in no way gave himself any respite,
but day and night he labored at the sweet honey of the divine books, by which he sweetened our language and our Church.
For he translated divine books whose enumeration is all but impossible; of these let us mention some, so that through them the faithful of Christ may come to know of the others as well.
For he did not translate only on Olympus and on the Holy Mountain, so that we might list the works one by one; he also translated in the imperial city, on the road, and in other such places.
So he translated, as we said: the Commentary on John's own [?] Gospel.
