All these books, and many more besides, were translated by our God-clothed father, and in this way he multiplied the talent that had been entrusted to him.
He translated most of the books mentioned above while his father John was still alive, and he carried all the care and burden of the monastery.
For, as we said above, the blessed John spent many years in sickness, and he served him in his infirmity day and night.

Then he spent fourteen years as abbot. The care of three hundred souls, the management of the great lavra, and the greater part of the affairs of the Athonites were handled by that blessed man, and he also kept his own great and heavy rule of discipline strictly.
Along with all this, he did not set aside the good labour of translation, nor did he give himself any rest,
but he always toiled and kept vigil through the nights, for he translated most of the books at night by candlelight, as we said, because he had so little free time and so many duties.
While father John was still alive, a certain monk from the land of the Romans came, a man renowned for his virtue. He came with six of his disciples to this holy mountain to pray.
When our fathers saw his face adorned with grace, they greeted him as one of their own and someone they knew, received him with joy, and begged him to stay here, saying:
"We too are foreigners, and you too are a foreigner." With difficulty they persuaded him, for they wanted to be together in the monastery.
But since he was a prominent and famous man, when the Romans who were in the imperial city and in other cities learned of it, many people gathered to be made monks by him.
Then our fathers advised that holy elder, saying:
"Holy father, since you are bringing so many souls to salvation, it is better that you tonsure them, become the means of life for their souls, and offer them to God.
Know that still more people are going to come to receive the monastic habit from your hands. We will buy you a place and help you with everything you need."
Although disturbance and worry were burdensome to that holy man, he did not want to disobey their command.
So he built a beautiful monastery and gathered many brothers, and with the support of our fathers he completed all the work of building.
He would come to visit them again and again, stay many days, and then go back to his own monastery.

That monastery is the only monastery of the Romans on the Holy Mountain today, and they live well and in good order according to the rule and discipline of Saint Benedict, whose life is written in the Dialogues.
The worthy priest Gabriel the Georgian, who was mentioned earlier, and this great holy elder Leo the Roman had a great spiritual love for each other.
Whenever Leo came to visit the fathers, he had a cell near Gabriel's cell, and he spent those days there. Neither of them knew any language other than his own.
When it grew dark, they would come out of their cells, pray, sit down, and talk of divine things until the bell rang for matins.
They did this every evening until Leo left.
Our fathers said: "There were spiritual brothers around them, and they assured us under oath that:
"Whenever the great Leo came, he and Gabriel the priest always did this," and they testified that:
"Because of their holiness everything was possible and believable, for they were great and perfect before God."
In those days there was a certain catholicos of Thessalonica, a godly and spiritual man, a friend of our fathers.
Father Euthymius was in the habit of going to him many times, and sometimes the catholicos would bring him by insistence.
Now there was in Thessalonica a certain Jew learned in the Law, and the catholicos wanted to convert him to Christianity, and he talked with him again and again.
While Father Euthymius was with him, the catholicos asked him to speak with that Jew. When they had called him, they began to debate about the Law.
When that Jew was hard pressed and left helpless before the blessed Father Euthymius, he began to blaspheme the spotless faith of the Christians.
When Father Euthymius heard this, he was grieved and grew angry, and said to him: "Let your mouth be shut, you foul Jew!"
At that very moment he became mute, and his mouth was twisted. Other Jews were also standing there, and they fell at the feet of Father Euthymius, asking him to forgive him.
He answered: "Let him be forgiven by the one whom he blasphemed, and let him come to the faith; as for me, I have forgiven him."
Then the catholicos asked him to forgive him and to pray. When he had prayed and made the sign of the cross over him, at that very moment his mouth was restored and he began to speak.
At once he fell at his feet and became a Christian, and he proved to be a man of great faith.
Another Jew too, learned in the Law, highly educated and famous for disputation, came to Father Euthymius with Jewish arrogance and wanted to debate.
The blessed man was reluctant to do this, but at John's command he was compelled to speak with him.
When the man began to dispute and question, Euthymius explained and expounded everything to him beyond all understanding.
When that crafty man saw that he was defeated, he began to speak words of blasphemy.
This displeased the blessed man, and he said to him: "If you were asking about the word of the Scriptures, we would explain it to you, and
if you were asking about us, we would answer you; but since you speak blasphemy against the Most High, let your blaspheming mouth be shut!"
When he heard this, he became mute at once, and the next day he gave up his soul.
Once there was a severe drought, and May, June, July and August passed without rain,
and the land suffered greatly, so that even the leaves of the trees and the vines dried up and fell, and people were in great distress.
Our monastery has a small monastery on the mountain, where a church of the holy prophet Elijah is built.
When the feast of Saint Elijah came, one day beforehand Father John commanded his son Euthymius:
"Take the brothers with you and go to the church of Saint Elijah, spend the night there and celebrate the liturgy."
When he gave him this command, many brothers were gathered before Father John, and he commanded him as if in jest, saying:
"Boys, take your rain cloaks with you, for I trust in God that we will not come back for nothing."
They set out and spent the night there. When the hour of the liturgy came, our holy father Euthymius put on his vestments.
As they began the prayers, before the reading of the Gospel, a small cloud appeared over Hierissos.
At that very moment the sky filled with clouds. Before the time of communion, a terrible rain fell and soaked the whole land.
When they saw this, they raised their hands and gave thanks to God. When they had finished the liturgy and taken food, they came back home.
The brothers who had rain cloaks came down to the monastery cheerfully, but those who had none came down with toil and hardship.
So both groups alike gave thanks to God and to the blessed father John.
Once our holy father Euthymius wanted to go up the mountain of Athos for the feast of the Transfiguration,
since it is the custom of the monks of the Holy Mountain that a great crowd of people gathers on the summit of the mountain for this feast and keeps vigil through the night.
When they had spent the night, the hour of the liturgy came, and our holy father Euthymius put on his vestments, and the other priests with him did too.
When they had brought in the holy gifts and lifted them up at the "Holy" [?], they saw our father Euthymius as if he were a blazing fire. Dread seized them all.
At that same moment a sound was heard like the shouting of a great crowd. The mountain shook with a great earthquake, and everyone fell on their faces.
When father Euthymius raised them up, they were like dead men from fear.
When he saw them so terrified, he said to them: "Do not be afraid, brothers. This was a divine visitation, and Christ has glorified his own feast."
Then they were all comforted and gave glory to God.
Among the sees with the rank of catholicos, a notable and eminent one is the see of Saint Epiphanius of Cyprus.
In the time of Emperor Basil, the archbishop of that see died, and the emperor pressed the blessed Euthymius hard to take over its government.
But he refused outright to take it on, because with all eagerness he fled from human glory and the turmoil of the world, and he held humility dear.
Since our blessed father Euthymius was full of grace from on high, he likewise laid down godly rules and ordinances for his monastery:
first, the rules of the church services and the order for the whole year, as they are written in the great Synaxarion, completely and without omission.
He was always urging the brothers to be eager to go to church, to stand there in good order, and to pray fervently.
The blessed man's own dwelling was up high, on top of a tall tower, and yet no one ever arrived at the morning prayer before him.
He would stand in church with all diligence and reverence, without a staff and without leaning against the wall.
Whenever there was some small matter to deal with, he would give the order to his disciple privately, and the disciple would go.
Whether the order was for the steward or for the assistant steward, the disciple would quietly draw him aside, take him out to the [?] (štosa), and tell him the father's order there.
And when there was something important, he would go out himself to the portico [?] and talk there. Inside the church, no one would ever dare to talk at all.
And although the brothers stand by the wall, no one leans against the wall. For they too imitated that blessed one as far as they were able.
The young men were assigned to stand in the middle of the church, and they stand in two or three rows, with their hands folded and with reverence.
And benches are set in the middle, and when it is proper they sit in the same way, in two or three rows.
And when the dean (dekanos) or the sacristan calls someone to read a book, or to come forward, or to any other service of the church,
he goes up to him from the side, bows to him, and tells him so that only he hears. And the other bows and goes off to his service.
Two epiteretai, that is, overseers, were appointed. They were godly and God-fearing men:
one senior, and one junior under him, whom the senior sends to the brothers' cells to bring in those who have stayed behind.
If anyone does not come at the appointed time of matins, he is given a fitting penance, as the father had ordained.
And for those who worked hard all day and had no time to sleep, he counted their day's labour as prayer.
But as for those who were either at leisure or in light duties, whether priests, deacons or chanters: if they were young,
they made a hundred prostrations before the altar. But if they were old and weak, he ordered them to go without wine and food [?] for that day.

During prayer, the senior epiteretes always stands at the doors of the church and asks the brothers who go out their reason for leaving. Unless someone had very urgent business, no one would dare to go out.
But if something was urgent, he would tell the epiteretes and come back again quickly.
But if he delayed, the epiteretes would rebuke him severely and warn him: "Do not do this again!"
And if he still did it, the epiteretes would not let him into the refectory. Instead, he ordered him to eat only dry bread that day, or to make a hundred prostrations.
For those who laboured and were worn out, the father ordained that after the appointed services they could leave and rest until the second bell, and then come back to the church again.
But if they were negligent, the epiteretai would bring them.
If any brothers quarrelled, the father would summon them and see them. Not being disobedient to his command, they would make peace.
But if they were found to be hard-hearted and persisted in it, it was ordained
that they should not enter the refectory until they were reconciled, and should take only bread [?] and water. And if the superior was not present, the steward (oikonomos) would impose the penance.
Whenever they went into the church, first Father Euthymius and then all the brothers, until they had knelt down and venerated the holy Mother of God that is above the doors,
they would not enter. And whenever the brothers passed before the father, whether in church or anywhere else, they would not pass by until they had knelt and bowed humbly.
And in the same way, our blessed father Euthymius would bow low not only to men of rank but even to those who had just arrived, and he greeted them kindly.
And if he saw zealous brothers who took care for their souls, he would give no commands at all to such as these.
But if he saw any who were negligent, slack, or newly arrived, he would speak to them again and again and teach them,
rebuke and comfort them, and entrust them to the officials, so that they would treat them kindly and put no burden on them.
Once they had said the evening prayers, the brothers were not allowed to gather in a cell to talk, or to talk anywhere in the monastery.
And if the overseers found anyone doing so, they would quiet them and send them off to their own cells.
But if anyone dared to resist them, the father would give the order and quickly impose a penance on him.
Whenever they saw any of the young brothers talking with one another, laughing, or touching one another's hands, they would rebuke them at once.
And if they did it a second time, they would report it to the father, and he would impose a heavy penance.
If something happened through the work of the enemy, such as a violent quarrel between brothers, tearing at each other's beards, or grappling with one another, it was the custom of our father,
in whom there was no shouting or unruly anger, since he was adorned with every virtue, to talk with them in sweet and gentle words, drawing on the books and speaking from memory.
And he would say to them: "Children, if I let you off in this matter, first you will destroy your own souls, and then the monastery will fall into disorder. Since it has come about
that God has appointed me as your judge and governor, know that if I let you off without correction, you will be bitterly judged in the age to come.
But if I correct you a little here and you accept it with thanks, I trust in God that you will be delivered from that eternal judgment."
After persuading them in this way, he would learn from the brothers what had really happened. If both were at fault, he punished both, and if only one, then that one.
The punishment matched the quarrel: if it was serious, he punished severely, and if it was minor, lightly. He would bring the brother to the father's quarters and order him to lie face down.
And that brother would bow and lie face down on the ground.
One brother would hold his head, another his feet, and others would strike him over his robe with a strap: some thirty times, some forty, and some sixty.
But if anyone was found to be a partisan [?] and to have helped one side against the other, he was greatly angered and punished him severely.
After the beating, those who had been beaten would kneel and bow down, and with tears ask the father's forgiveness.
Some spent two weeks lying down afterward, and some three.
From time to time the father would visit and comfort them in word and deed. He would send them delicacies and entrust them to the officials, so that they would look after them and comfort them.
And anyone he had punished without any cause, he would comfort and build up with a robe, a cowl, or some other necessary thing.
There was no grumbling or loss of heart at all among those who had been beaten. Instead they regarded it as if they had been disciplined by the hands of Christ.
Our holy father Euthymius had this custom: on three days of the week, Monday, Wednesday, and Friday,
he took bread and water in his cell at sunset, except on the great feasts. On the other days he always went to the refectory,
except when someone from the Lavra or the Protos came. On those occasions the brothers had arranged to prepare a meal separately, either in the father's quarters or wherever he wished,
so that the brothers' meal would not be delayed because of the work, for the brothers were very heavily occupied with labour at that time.
Our blessed father never drank wine, except at the liturgy or for some serious reason, until he was old.
But whenever he sat at table, he had ordered the refectorian always to set before him a cup of the brothers' wine. And he would taste it.
If it was good, he would say nothing. But if it was vinegary, or had too much water mixed into it, then after rising from the table he would speak to the wine-steward and say:
"Brother, these brothers have no other consolation from anywhere except this table.
If the wine is light, do not add any water to it at all. If it is middling, add as much as is proper. And if it is better, add as is fitting."
In the same way, although he himself ate none of it, he would have the brothers' food brought before him and taste it too.
If it lacked oil, he would speak to the cellarer and order him to correct it. But if it was undercooked [?], or unsalted, or too salty,
then when he rose from the table he would speak to the cook and tell him: "Do your service in the fear of God, brother, and do not say,
'I am serving men.' Instead, think of it as if you were serving the angels of God, so that you do not lose your reward."
It was our father's rule never to speak at all at table, unless there were guests present, and even then he would rarely give a quiet answer,
or if he wanted water, or if he was sending a blessing to someone.
Or if some necessary matter came up at table, he would call a disciple and give him orders privately, so that no one else would know.
None of the other brothers would ever dare to speak. As for the refectorian and the servers, if there was some necessary matter, they would whisper privately.
It was the same with the brothers: if there was some necessary matter, whether they were asking for water or for anything else, they asked privately.
This too had been laid down for the refectorian: "If you see anyone talking, or laughing, or behaving frivolously at table, send him word, saying:
'Do not do that any more. Otherwise, the father has ordered me to lead you outside.'"
If anyone was found doing this, whether because of the Enemy or because of drink, and started talking or making merry again, the father had announced to the brothers in church:
"I have instructed the refectorian, and no one is to resist him when he leads someone outside."
No one dared to resist, and the refectorian would lead such a person outside until he had learned his lesson.
Serving duty was assigned to the workers on feast days and Sundays, or when there was bad weather. On working days, those who stayed indoors, and the priests and deacons, did the serving,

as it fell to their turn, along with the other people who were free. It was our father's rule that if some important matter came up, whether from the king or from the court, he would consult the brothers in the church.

If there was some matter for the community, he would call the brothers who had knowledge of that matter, whether it was smithing, carpentry, or vineyard work, and he would manage the monastery's affairs together with them.
Other small matters, however, he would discuss with the steward. For although our thrice-blessed father Euthymius was knowledgeable in every matter,
in his great humility he did nothing without asking advice.
And even in his old age he would not allow himself to enter the church with a staff.
But for the weak brothers a rule was set: they stand in the side aisle of the church, leaning on their staffs.
And those who were especially weak were told to sit on benches in that same aisle.
And more than anything our holy father hated this: when some people falsely said something, either about the church or about some brother.
And for this reason he gave a firm order that, unless they knew a thing for certain, they should not dare to mention it at all.
But if anyone reported something falsely, he would impose a heavy penance on them.
And for this reason he sent many brothers away from the monastery, "so that the community may be at peace," he said.

Two or three times a month, on Sundays, he would feed the brothers with spiritual teaching. Since he was full of the grace of God, he taught them from the holy Scriptures what would benefit their souls.
And they would all be so moved that they shed many tears and gave thanks to God, and they received his word as if it were Christ's.
He taught them about love and humility, about obedience and reverence, about meekness and calm,
about patience and service, about going to church promptly, and about keeping all the other rules of the community with zeal.
And he would say to them: "Brothers, let us work hard so that our gathering in this holy place is not useless, and so that our departure from this world is not in vain."
And he would tell them many other teachings, as God put them into his mouth.
And the brothers were kept free from worry about every bodily need, because he gave them everything, down to the [?] (perhaps the awl or the thread) and the needle.
And every excuse was taken away, so that no one would worry about anything, or sell, or buy, or get anything for himself, or acquire anything without his order.
And if someone wanted to give something to a brother, no one dared to give it without the father's order, unless he had first asked him.
And if anyone broke his commandment and bought a garment or anything else, or acquired money, he would rebuke him at once and impose a severe penance.
And many times we saw him burn things inside the monastery enclosure, whether signet rings, a garment, or a cowl.
For there was an archdeacon, a worthy man and the son of distinguished parents, who had given the monastery no small amount of money, along with his own vestment,
which had been placed in the church. He did not want anyone to wear it except himself.
One day our holy father wished to offer the bloodless sacrifice, and he told another archdeacon
to put on the tunic, the vestment of the archdeacon mentioned earlier.
But he answered: "Spiritual father, the brother may be upset, because he does not want anyone to wear his tunic."
When the father heard this, he called that archdeacon and said to him gently and kindly:
"Will you allow this brother to put on your tunic and serve at the altar with us?"
And he saw that he was upset and did not want to put it on. And when he had finished the holy liturgy,
he called the archdeacon mentioned above and said to him: "Tell me the truth: what have you left behind in the world?"
And he said to him: "Holy father, your worthiness knows well
that I have left behind parents and brothers, and money and no small possessions. And what I have handed over into your holy hands, you yourself know."
Our father said to him: "And do you think it right, son, to lose the grace and reward for all of that over this tunic of yours?"
And he said: "God forbid, father." And at once he ordered fire to be brought, and with his own hand he threw the tunic into the fire.
And so it was burned. And the brother fell at his holy feet and asked forgiveness.
And in the same way, if anyone had a garment or any other useful thing and did not want to let his brother use it when he needed it, he would likewise burn it with fire and say to him:
"Have we not been commanded to lay down our lives for our brothers? And you prefer a perishable thing to your brother, and are you not ashamed?"
And they received his teaching like a medicine of life, and gave thanks to God, who had granted them such a physician of souls.
He always taught the brothers: "It would be right for us to seek nothing beyond the common table, since we know
with what hardship all the saints passed through this transient life, so that they did not even satisfy themselves with water, men of whom this world was not worthy,
innocent and spotless and holy, free of every sin. But we, who are full of every sin,
is the comfort of the common table not enough for us, receiving food twice a day, fully and without any lack, with wine and food? Truly it is enough, and more than enough.
But since we do not want to put even a little constraint on ourselves, and we make many excuses, if anyone cannot be content with the table alone,
and either I or the official gives him something he needs, let him use it alone by himself and not lead another brother into fault.
And if he does not do this, God will require the guilt of both of them from him."
Moreover, buying wine or fish was never even mentioned in the monastery, except for oil,
and even that only for those who were readers or scribes, who burned it for reading or for writing.
There was no other custom of lighting a lamp or setting up icons in the cells.
Instead, one cross or one icon was set up, so that when they prayed they could bow down before them and kiss them.
And if anyone bought oil or wine without the father's word, they poured it out into the latrine.
And no one cooked food for himself except in serious illness, for the father would go into the kitchen,
and if he saw pots at the edge of the fire, he would ask the cook whose they were. And if they belonged to the sick, he would leave them alone.
But if anyone had made it out of gluttony, sometimes he ordered it poured out, and sometimes poured in with the food for the laypeople.
Many citizens, and people from other places too, would come with great wealth in order to be tonsured.
He would detain them for some time and give them rest, and then he would tell them: "Forgive us, we cannot tonsure you.

You are men of renown, and we are poor men and strangers. When you give wealth to the church, you will want to live in comfort, and perhaps we will not be able to give you comfort, and then you will be aggrieved.
And besides, all the brothers labour hard, and if some were to stay idle, they too would be aggrieved."
In this way he sent many away, and they left. But if a brother came who was a hard worker and humble, the father would say:
"Believe me, brothers, I would rather receive these than have someone give me a thousand drachmas."
From the beginning there were eminent men: Hilarion Kananakhi, deacon of the Resurrection.
He had come here when the monastery was first being built, and the monastery was built under his stewardship, and our fathers regarded him as their own brother.
He begged them to let him go to Jerusalem. They sent him there, and he spent many years in the diaconate.
The fathers wrote to him many times and brought him back here again.
On both his first coming and his second, what he brought in silver, gold, silk and [?] (sakhedari) came to more than twenty litrai.
They gave him a disciple and set him an allowance apart from his own [?] (krasovuli): one jar of wine a month, one cheese, three litrai of oil, and one loaf of bread a day. This was his allowance.
Next came Girpeli, chief of the treasurers of Jojik, and he was baptised, for he was an Armenian. They named him Arsenius.
His own nephew, his sister's son, served him. After many years he again asked leave to go and see the sons of his lord.
Over his two comings he brought more than fifteen litrai and gave it to the monastery. They gave him the same allowance as Kananakhi.
Next came Athanasius of Peritheorion with his son. He was very useful to the church. He had a monastery at Karyes, and they gave it to our fathers along with a great deal of other wealth.
The fathers sold that monastery for three hundred and forty drachmas, and he had the same allowance as Kananakhi.
In those times, whenever such a man came, he would give half of his wealth to the church and half to the poor.
On top of the ascetic labours of our holy father, the affairs of the people and the translation of books, he also bore this great burden of care, for neither the protos
nor the other abbots did anything without his command, and rarely did a day pass without ten or fifteen abbots coming before them.
The care of the Great Lavra, a heavy and many-sided task, was also on him, for the great Athanasius had entrusted him with its affairs, its oversight and its governance.
On top of his labours and struggles, whenever there was some practical work to be done for the monastery, he would go out with them unless he was busy, whether to haul up a boat,
or when a boat came with wheat, or to stake the vines, or for [?] (ajojva), or for [?] (siuleba).
Since the vineyards had only recently been planted, they all needed tending with stakes.
They spent most days working in the vineyards, and the father was always with them, unless there was some serious reason.
And again, because of the burghals [?], all the villages were in distress and almost empty of people.
And to make up for the hardship, more sowing was done in the mountains with the hoe: satsune [?], emmer wheat and flax, and the mowing of hay.
And the brothers worked hard at all this. Since all of them took part, it was not a burden to them; they did it without grumbling and with joy.
And the father went to all these works again and again, and comforted them with word and deed, and with food and drink.
Our blessed father always used to say to the steward: "Do not take on beardless workers, because they are in some way harmful to the brothers:
some are harmed in their thoughts and some by looking. Do not worry at all about losing money.
It is better for us to lose ten or fifteen drachmas than for some harm to come to the brothers."
Likewise, if any of the brothers brought beardless relatives of their own, the father was also willing for them to learn letters and a craft.
But he would not keep them in the monastery. Instead he would send them out to the villages, wherever he knew there was a better, spiritual and experienced steward, and they were brought up there.
And when they had grown beards, he would bring them into the monastery.
In the mule stable all the muleteers were brothers. Two laymen served there as servants and sweepers, and the rest were brothers.
And it was not a burden to them; rather, they rejoiced, because their souls were watered by the teaching and instruction of our holy father. For he always used to say:
"Those who live in a community are saved by these three things: humility, obedience, and giving up their own will."
And when he saw one of the brothers careless and drowsy at prayer in church, he would ask him: "Why do you sleep in church?
Is sleeping in your cell not enough for you?" And if the brother told him, "I keep vigil in my cell, and that is why sleep overcomes me," he would order him:
"That, beloved, is a snare of the enemy, meant to make you lose something great for the sake of something small.
God requires of a person who goes to church that he stand there alert and with a contrite heart.
If you cannot do this, then keep vigil in church and take your fill of sleep in your cell, and do not sleep here. Otherwise I will give you a heavy penance."
As gatekeeper of the monastery he always appointed a careful and spiritual man.

And the gatekeeper was instructed as follows: if monks came from distant [?] places of this region, and they arrived in the evening, they were to have supper and eat the midday meal, and then he was to send them off and charge them not to come at an improper hour.
And the cellarers were ordered to give hospitality to the laymen and to send them off.
And at the cellar door there was by no means to be any gathering [?], because of passions of many kinds.
But if strangers came, the gatekeeper was ordered to send them off on the third day, after the meal.
Indeed, no one at all ever dared to gather at the gates, to hold meetings inside the monastery, or to engage in useless talk in the cells.

The rule for the cellar was set as follows: they were not to cook food there, unless there were strangers or some workers. For these they would sometimes prepare it on the spot and sometimes in the kitchen, and carry it there.
At the midday meal the cellarers always went to the refectory, one to the first table and the other to the second table.
The wine-stewards did the same. But if the cellarers needed anything in the evening, they had it indoors.
Above all, concerning the epistates, who is the chief of the workers, Father Euthymius urged them and told them:
"Let the epistates lack nothing, so that he is not distressed and does not lead thirty or forty workers astray.
And these [?] treasure [?], which it is our duty to give them." The disciples of the cell-companions went out to every kind of secular work.
The cook was ordered to prepare their food for them. If there was no necessary task, his disciples also went with the brothers to work.

Most often the cell-companions themselves also went out with the brothers, out of goodwill toward the brothers, especially when the father was there. The storehouse, the garden and the mills were the cellarer's responsibility.
Whatever anyone needed from these, the cellarer took care of it together with the steward and the superior.

But the assistant steward's office, the shoemakers' workshop, the mule stable, the smithy, the carpenters, the caulkers, the sheepfolds, the vineyards and the boatmen were the steward's responsibility.
The cellarer had no authority over the vineyards with regard to the grapes. In the same way the steward had no authority over the fruit. Whether inside the monastery
or outside on the dependent estates, the fruit was the cellarer's responsibility, whether it was olives, walnuts or other fruit.
But whenever anything needed to be given away, the steward consulted the cellarer.
When the fruit ripened, the cellarers went out again and again to the dependent estates. They inspected the orchards, showed them to the people living there, and instructed them:
"Inside and outside, this is greatly needed by the brothers and the church. Keep back only what you need to get by, and take nothing more from it."
They did not dare do anything improper. Everything went into the cellar, and the cellarer had plenty to give to the refectory and to send wherever it was needed.
But if the cellarer, the monks or the laymen needed anything, the steward gave it.

When the father was at home, anyone who needed anything reported it to the father himself, and no one asked the steward for anything. If someone did ask him, he sent that person to the father. But when the father was not at home, the steward saw to it.
The steward's fixed allowance was seven cups of wine, and when he sat down at table in the evening, they brought him four cups.
If he was not at home, the father had ordered: "Prepare one dish for him, and give him fruit, olives and whatever he asks for." Whatever was left over, he sent back to the cellar.
At that time the rule was that the superior had ordered the cellar to give the brothers and the craftsmen what they needed, whether their fixed ration or more, if anyone asked for it.
For this reason no one went to the steward for anything when the father was not at home. But if any guests came, the steward looked after them.
Other necessities they requested from the steward: [?], [?], leather, ropes or flax. Things of that kind they requested from the steward.
In this way every matter was put in order, and everyone lived without disturbance.
To the monastery's farm estates, such as Sisikon, Karavan, Theologos and others like them, they gave from the monastery everything needed for their own running [?]. Whatever was produced there,
they brought all of it down, except for a certain amount that they left to the people living there for their own needs.

Again, for those who live in cells [?] our holy father made this rule: if any bread was left over to them, they did not have authority to give it away anywhere, but were to give it back to the cellarer.
There were both inside and outside [the monastery] spiritual and God-clad fathers:
the blessed Arsenius of Ninotsminda, the holy elder John Grdzelisdze, the Spirit-clad elder John the Recluse, and others who imitated them,
men enlightened by grace from on high and imitators of the angels in their way of life.
Besides their other virtues, they did this too in their old age: the father could in no way persuade them to take the bread and wine meant for the sick.
Instead they were content with the brothers' bread and, if they needed it, with their cup of wine.
Although they had given the monastery no small offering, they would not agree to take anything beyond what was necessary and the meager needs of the body.
Also, all our nobles had great faith in their holiness and many times brought gifts before them.
They would take these in hand and bless them, and then send them on to the father just as they were, still sealed. Many times the father begged them
to give some of it to the poor, or wherever they wished. But those blessed men said to him:
"Holy father, we are spiritual subjects of the church, and God does not require such deeds from those who are under obedience."
As for the bread they took from the monastery, they did not give any of it to the poor either, but said, "The monastery feeds the poor."
But if they had fruit, or vegetables, or drink, or something of that kind, they would give it to the poor.
And if bread was left over, they would not take the next week's portion.
Also, on ordinary days each of them struggled on his own, like the bodiless ones, but on feasts and Sundays they performed the rule of prayer together and broke their fast together.
To see their way of life was truly like seeing the angels of God, and their speech was orderly and sweet.
So they completed their lives, and, perfect in every virtue, they passed away into the presence of God. They rejoice with all the saints and ask God for mercy on our behalf.
Our God-clad father Euthymius truly testified about them:
"In these last, vain times, men so perfect and so lofty in virtue will no longer appear." For there was no virtue that they did not possess perfectly, to a high degree, and without fault.
Their purified bodies, worn out with labor, were laid in a tomb in front of the church of Saint Symeon the Elder,
in a single burial chamber, near their own cells of ascetic struggle, which are at Karavai [?].
Beliar, the enemy of the saints, who envies the salvation of humankind, saw these spiritual rules
that our father Euthymius had established, and the progress of the brothers, and the translation of divine books. He burned with rage and was consumed with envy.
He found a certain wretched man, a monk in appearance, and stirred him up to kill the saint.
For he appeared to him and said, "If you kill my enemy Euthymius, I will do great good for you."
So he got a sword ready and meant to kill him, but God brought his plan to nothing.
For one day, when he had gone up to the tower, the disciple closed the door and was himself going down to his own cell.
When he had gone a little way down the stairs of the tower, that maddened monk met him and said, "I am going up to the father; let me in to him [?]."
But he said to him, "It is not proper to go up to the father like this, at an untimely hour."
And the monk said, "I cannot possibly not go up." And since that blessed disciple of the father would not let him go up,
the madman at once drew that devilish sword and mercilessly cut down that blessed brother, and then he himself ran off to get away.
As he was running away, another disciple of the father also met him, and he cut him down with the sword as well.
When there was shouting and an uproar, our holy father learned of this. He went down at once, completed them with the monastic schema, and gave them communion of the holy mysteries.
And so, adorned with the crown of martyrdom, they departed this life and went before God.
That savage man confessed that his impulse came from the enemy. As his wickedness deserved, his wretched soul left him in bitter torment.
At another time the devil stirred up the monastery's gardener and put it into his mind, too, to kill the holy man.
But as soon as he set his hand to it, his hand became useless and stayed like a dried-up piece of wood, until he confessed everything. Through the saint's prayer he was healed, and he glorified God.
Along with all his other virtues he also had this great virtue: he did nothing at all without discernment, for he used to say:
"Trusting in oneself and following one's own will destroys the soul, but discernment is the guide of life, as our holy fathers have said."
And he kept to this rule until the end of his life.

Our holy father Euthymius was calm in appearance. In mind he was simple and humble, and in soul he was enlightened and pure. In body he was strong in divine works and ascetic labours, and he was well proportioned in stature.
He would not affirm or say anything on his own authority without the testimony of the Scriptures. He stood steadfastly in church,
for he stood without a staff and without leaning against the wall, with his hands joined, like an unshakable pillar.
And his face and eyes were turned toward the ground.
As for his labours in his cell, who could count them? God alone knew them, for he carried them all out in secret.
His clothing was a hair shirt, and over the hair shirt a heavy chain.
Whatever virtue anyone might look for, he would find it in him, practised well and beautifully.
He kept his purity and virginity untouched and spotless, like an angel of God dwelling in heaven.
And above all his virtues he had the translation of books, as a crown and a source of enlightenment for our nation.
Our holy father Euthymius completed fourteen years after the death of his father,
…in the abbacy. Later, at the entreaty of the holy elders mentioned above, Bishop Arsenius and John Grdzelisdze, he stepped down from the abbacy.
For those worthy elders saw that his many different cares were keeping him from translating the holy Scriptures. So he freed himself of them and settled in his own cell.
He entrusted the abbacy of the brethren to George, his own kinsman, about whom Father John had left instructions.
He himself devoted himself to translating divine books, and he translated a great many books, some of which we have mentioned above.
He still had the care of the Great Lavra, however, and as long as they obeyed him, he governed it well.
But at last they began to be self-willed and rebellious and to change abbots one after another, and their rebellion grew more and more,
until they went up to the imperial city and informed Emperor Constantine about their turmoil.
When the emperor learned that the great Euthymius was their governor, he summoned him to the imperial city,
so that he might learn the whole truth from him, for he had great faith in him and love for him because of his worthiness.
As he was setting out to go before the emperor, he gathered all the brethren and comforted them, prepared a good table for them, and commended himself to their prayers.
Then he went to the blessed priest Theophanes, a doer of Christ's will, for whom Father Euthymius had great love,
for he had been raised here from his youth and was adorned with every virtue.
He was a priest pleasing to the Lord, very learned, and a skilled scribe of divine books. Father Euthymius testified about him:
"He has written books for the monastery, inside and outside, worth more than one thousand five hundred drachmas."
After Arsenius and John died, our father often consulted him on spiritual matters.
So he went to this blessed elder, greeted him with weeping, and commended himself to his prayers.
The elder embraced him and said with tears: "Woe is me, wretched one, for I shall never again see you in the flesh, O holy father!"
Father Euthymius himself also confirmed his words. And this indeed came to pass, and the prophecy of both was fulfilled.

For, as we have said, our God-clad father Euthymius went up to the imperial city. When the emperor learned that he had come, he received him with great honor and asked him about the affairs of the Lavra.
Much time passed before all the business was settled, and the feast of Saint John the Theologian arrived. As was his custom,
he celebrated it splendidly and provided for many poor people. He gave good comfort to the monks who were with him, served them himself in person, and filled them with every good thing.
After this he himself broke his fast and rested a little from his labor.
When he got up, he remembered the icon of Saint John the Evangelist, which had been given to a painter to be adorned. He ordered a disciple to go and tell the painter how it should be fitted out.
Then he said: "Perhaps you will not be able to make him understand the way we need it, son. Instead, put me on a mount, and I will go myself."
But that mule had just been bought and was vicious, and they did not know how wild and bad-tempered it was.
After some time had passed, he came upon a poor man who was begging for alms, and our holy father stopped so that he could give him alms.
The man, dressed in rags, got up and came toward him to receive the alms.
But when that vicious mount saw him, it shied at once, began to bolt, and lunged this way and that, until it badly injured our holy and blessed father.
When it had thrown him down, a great crowd gathered around him, for everyone knew him, and they all wept and mourned.
Then they carried him to the monastery where he had been staying.
When the emperor Constantine heard of it, he was greatly distressed, and he sent one of his own close attendants to ask after him.
The citizens, the nobles, the officials, and the members of the palace also had great faith in him and love for him. They all came, bathed in tears, kissed him, and went away.
And what can anyone say about the Georgians? They never left that angel-like body of his at all, and with loud lamentations they mourned their orphanhood.
So, in prayer and in thanksgiving to God, our thrice-blessed and God-clothed father Euthymius passed away, and great grief came upon us,
since we had lost that sweet and beloved father of ours. But he went before God, into the light that no shadow touches,
together with all the saints who have pleased God since the beginning of time, and he intercedes for the salvation of our souls before the Holy Trinity.
His precious relics were brought up to his own monastery and placed in a burial casket in the church of Saint John the Baptist.
Those who approach them in faith are abundantly filled with the grace of healing, through the boldness he has before God.
Our thrice-blessed father Euthymius died on the thirteenth of the month of May, on a Monday,
in the eleventh indiction, in the year six thousand five hundred and thirty-six from the creation of the world,
to the glory of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, to whom belong glory and honor, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
Now, after our holy father Euthymius had given up the leadership of the monastery and, as we said above, had appointed George as father,
George gradually changed most of the rules mentioned above. He followed his own will and plans and wanted to establish some other rules and canons.
Although this troubled the great Euthymius, he was a lover of peace and full of love,
so he did not dispute with him at all. Instead, he kept carefully to his own service and devoted himself to translating divine books.
George, for his part, was shrewd in worldly affairs and was well known among the nobles and officials of that time, and the whole Mountain greatly honored and respected him.

He also became very fond of the Greeks. He increased their number and turned wholly toward them. The Georgians, on the other hand, he treated as castoffs of some kind and as worthless: he disregarded them and reduced their number.
For, as you all know, we are quickly unsettled and are quick to start wandering here and there, and for this reason we do great harm both to our own souls and to the place.
Since he was a cautious and serious man, he could not put up with excessive familiarities [?] and flatteries. And moreover, since he saw
since a great many people were needed for the extent of the monastery and the great number of services, and we were not enough, he turned to the Greeks and increased their number.
However, since one must speak the truth: if some Georgian came who was able to serve in the community, he would provide whatever he needed
in every way. And if he did not wish to live in the community, he would settle him wherever he wished to settle among the hermitages [?] of the monastery.
He refused bread to no Georgian. And men such as Gregory the Black, Zacharias son of Mirdat, Arsenius and others like them
he honored with great honor, visited with kindness, and provided for as they wished.
And some time passed in this state of affairs.
And after this, in the time of Emperor Romanos, George became greatly distinguished before Emperor Romanos and was very close to him and much honored.
And then (how it happened, God knows) they accused him of rebellion and disloyalty toward Diogenes on account of certain people, concerning whom they said
that George wanted the kingship for one of them. For this reason George was exiled to Monobata, and he died there in exile.
And the monastery and all of us who had remained at that time fell into great turmoil and plunder,
for the monastery was plundered three times, and all the fine [?] things that our fathers had acquired were carried off as booty, and likewise the treasury and the fabrics.
And since the Greeks found such an opportunity, they set about using every means to drive the Georgians out of this monastery.

And to this end they showed great zeal: they drew the whole Mountain to their side, won over all the nobles of Greece and the dignitaries of the palace, and brought much labor, affliction and toil upon us.
And to put it briefly: if the Lord had not helped us, along with the intercession of the holy Mother of God and the grace and prayers of our holy fathers,
today not a single Georgian would be found in this vast and glorious lavra,
which our holy fathers had built and raised up for us Georgians at very great expense and with much sweat.
And for this reason, so that this evil the Greeks brought upon us would not be forgotten, and so that those who come after us would not again fall into the same affliction,
all the brothers gathered together by common counsel, and with one mind we wrote this memorandum set down below, in this manner and form, in the time of Father Symeon. And we say this:
"Since, by the grace and mercy of God, our holy fathers John, John and Euthymius set out and came to this holy Mountain, as a haven for many souls and to increase
our nation; and with great struggle and at great expense they built this glorious lavra as a dwelling-place for Georgians; and then, through the service and favor of the God-serving Greek emperors,
in the time of the rebel Skleros, they enlarged and enriched it and acquired villages, monasteries and chrysobulls for it,
as is written above. And they fell asleep with a good end and departed to eternal life.
"And they left as heir and administrator the blessed Euthymius, who adorned this holy place with every good rule and with translations
He enlightened and adorned our nation and our language with the holy Scriptures, and for many years he shepherded well this flock entrusted to him, and,
since our land was very far away, and this glorious place was very large,
he took in Greeks as helpers and servants, innocently and sincerely, and so the number of Greeks in this lavra grew.
A short time later he withdrew from the office of abbot and appointed his kinsman George as father. He himself lived in quiet retreat.
The fame of his virtues and his worthiness spread through all of Georgia, and not only Georgia but the Greek lands as well.
For this reason many worthy and holy men came to him and were enlightened by the sight of him, for example:
John Grdzelisdze, Arsenius bishop of Ninotsminda, the venerable John of Khakhuli, Okropir, and others who imitated them; and later the blessed elder Gregory, a new Abraham in his love of guests.
Also Zachariah son of Mirdat, Arsenius and others who imitated them. Like a kind father, he held them dear and gave them every kind of rest and comfort.
So, living a way of life pleasing to God, he passed away to the Lord, as we mentioned above. He commended the Georgian brothers to Father George and Father Gregory.
"Not long afterwards Father George began to forget them.
He took no care at all for the flourishing of the Georgians. Instead he turned entirely to the Greeks and increased their numbers,
and some time later he died in exile, as we mentioned above.
The holy elder Gregory was a safe harbour and a comforter for the Georgian nation.
"But when Father George had died in exile and we had become very few, the Greeks saw their chance,
and they flared up against us like fires. They wanted to root us out completely and to seize our inheritance.
What made it worse was that the man who then held the office of abbot was on their side: the wicked George,
in no way better [?] than that earlier George who opposed the great Athanasius, although that one repented in the end.
For this reason we were in great distress, and they despised and hated us.
It is not even possible to tell everything one by one: how many insults, how many outrages and reproaches they heaped on us day after day.
We were in great grief, oppressed by beatings and floggings and by being called heretics. They even wanted to wipe out the very name of the builders.
"When the blessed Father Gregory saw all this, his heart burned within him and he was distressed out of compassion for us. He constantly begged God with tears to plan what was best for us.
While he was grieving like this, God gave us a man skilled in both and full of wisdom, the blessed Arsenius. He did not spare himself,
but did everything in his power to make our position secure, together with several other Christ-loving brothers. May their memory and their blessing last forever.
For it is not even possible to count one by one all the struggles they endured;
Our journeys by sea and by land, to Abkhazia and to Kartli, for letters of petition to the Greek emperors, and how many times we obtained a letter from the autocrats and came back.
And again they would drive us away with abuse and contempt, without provisions and without means [?], in the season of breaking waves and of winter.
And so, either by begging or through the mercy of God-loving men, we went up again to the imperial city, and again we wept before the emperors and pleaded our case before them.
And there God would again raise up patrons for us, who supported us, such as the Christ-loving brothers Chorchaneli and Parsman,
who greatly stretched out to us the hand of mercy. May the Lord repay them a thousandfold!
And while we were in these troubles, no small trials came upon the brothers day after day, and especially upon the blessed Arsenius,
for he was even beaten, and he endured much hardship, confinement in prison, reproach and mockery, and so did all the brothers.
But the holy elder Gregory would comfort us and give us courage, so that we would not lose heart.
"God the Almighty saw all this.
In his goodness he softened the heart of the Christ-loving Emperor Michael and turned him to mercy toward us. And after long hearings and investigations, our venerable father Gregory
he received with mercy, and by the will of God he again settled us in our place and dwelling, through the leadership and labours of Gregory and Arsenius and all our brothers,
who struggled even to the shedding of blood. And we gathered together and gave thanks to God, and we found rest from those many troubles.
"And some time passed, and Emperor Michael came to Thessalonica.
Again the Greeks were inflamed against us. They stirred up the whole Mountain and turned all the nobles, and they wanted
to make void and vain the earlier judgment and the mercy from God upon us.
But God frustrated their scheme and made their agitation vain,
for again God stretched out to us the hand of mercy, and the holy Mother of God did not drive us out of her temple, which they had attempted by every possible means,
so that, since they could not take the monastery from us, they might at least take the great church from us.
It was as if they even had a right to it, for they claimed that church had been theirs since it was built. And, as you see, its airiness and beauty surpass all praise,
so that on this Mountain, although there are a great many monasteries, nothing like it is found, and not only on the Mountain but in many other places as well.
But even so their attempt came to nothing, for the holy Mother of God granted to us poor ones that glorious temple of her glory,
and she always cares for us and protects us, her unworthy and foreign glorifiers and her flock.

And, as we have said, when they fought against us so heavily, the Christ-loving Emperor Michael again sat in judgment, and after thorough investigation he gave his ruling on both the church and the monastery, with all their property and wealth.
He granted them to us and poured great mercy and kindness on us. May Christ repay his soul a thousandfold!
"Father Gregory had died before this second judgment, and Arsenius died after this second judgment.
And of these many things we have recorded only a few.
"And since all this, and more than this, came upon us, and many of our brothers also turned away and went over to our adversaries,
we grew afraid because of all this, and we wrote down this record and left it for the generations who will come after us,
so that this great and many-sided turmoil will not be forgotten and cast aside.
And in full unity we say this, as with one mouth, together with all Georgians wherever they may be, in the East, on the Black Mountain and in Jerusalem, and wherever our brothers are:
If any man of our nation should appear, whether an abbot,
or a steward, or anyone else, who by any means or scheme, or out of greed for money, or out of love for the Greeks, or
out of favour toward some man, or by any other deceit, should be unfaithful to this holy place, or should give away land, whether on the mountain or outside it,
or should become a betrayer of the Georgians from within, and cut them off, and by some act of his own drive the Georgians out of this place, and expel them, and blot out our memory,

In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and through the intercession of the holy Mother of God, I, Father George,
during my time as abbot, moved the relics of Saint Euthymius from the church of the Baptist to the great church of the Mother of God. And I and the brothers set aside oil,
one metra each year, for the service at the tomb of those holy fathers, to be held in the month of May, on the 13th, the feast of this saint.
It is to be given to the sacristan, from one to the next in succession. And let no one dare to reduce it. Whoever does dare
will answer for it to God, to the holy father Euthymius, and to those holy fathers who were like him. And whoever adds to the service with zeal,
may his memory and blessing be eternal, through the intercession of our holy father Euthymius and of all his saints,
who from the beginning of the ages have been pleasing to our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever, amen.
Holy and God-clothed father Euthymius, have mercy on us, these your servants, pilgrims and poor,
in this foreign land, and ask forgiveness for us for our countless sins on that day of judgment, and in this life protect us from the snares of the devil and from the wiles of men.
O father, sweet in spirit and mind, may the memory of father George be everlasting, amen.
